title: Internalization thresholds and sales hooks for managed vs self-hosted inference
text:
Purpose:
Quick-reference GTM brief for AE/SDR/solutions when evaluating customers who are deciding whether to internalize inference (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM) or contract managed inference (Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private). Focus: concrete thresholds, common buyer claims, technical tradeoffs, and short rebuttal scripts + sales hooks.

Audience:
AEs, SEs, GTM product marketers, and Solutions Engineering. Use in discovery calls and early technical scoping. Keep this as a pragmatic checklist and conversation guide rather than a deep research paper.

Summary (one-paragraph):
Customers often believe self-hosting will save money and give control. In practice, there is a small but predictable window where internalization makes sense (very high sustained QPS, highly specialized hardware optimizations, or strict data residency/air-gap requirements). Outside that window, hidden operational costs, variability in tail latency, and continuous maintenance (kernel patches, quantization compatibility, model rollouts) tip the economics toward managed platforms. Redwood's strongest sales approach is to quantify the unknowns (FTEs, headroom, tail latency risk) and offer a transparent fallback path: predictable unit economics + hybrid options (Dedicated + Private) without losing control.

Decision thresholds (heuristic rules-of-thumb):
- Sustained tokens/month: < 10B tokens/month -> lean toward managed (hosted or dedicated) unless other constraints apply.
- Sustained peak QPS: > 4k concurrent generation QPS (short seq) -> consider Dedicated/self-host.
- Predictable vs spiky workload: if 95th pctile request volume spikes > 3x baseline frequently, managed burst/Dedicated recommended.
- Tail-latency SLO requirement: sub-200ms 99th for large context (4k+ tokens) is high risk for DIY unless you already operate optimized runtimes + NVLink topologies.
- Compliance/air-gap: if customer requires air-gapped on-prem with no outbound control plane, internalization may be required; Redwood Private is a bridge for customers wanting control with product support.

Typical hidden cost buckets for self-hosting (to use in economics conversation):
- Kernel/stack maintenance: 0.25-1.0 FTE per 100 GPUs initially rising with heterogeneity (GPU type + quantization)
- Model onboarding & compatibility testing: 0.5-2.0 FTEs for frequent model refresh cadence
- SRE/alerting/incident response: 1.0-2.5 FTEs depending on SLOs and 24/7 support needs
- Observability & Eval engineering: 0.5-1.0 FTE to keep quality/regression monitoring
- Opportunity cost of lost features: streaming, function-calling integrations, dynamic routing, and automatic fallbacks often need months of engineering to match managed feature parity
- Misc infra overhead: licensing for optimized kernels, NV switches, cluster networking, storage for KV caches, and GPU node churn (spares)

Concrete cost model snippet to use on-call (simple template):
- Infra monthly baseline (reserved instances + storage + networking): $X (customer input)
- Ops FTE cost monthly (FTEs * fully-burdened rate): $Y
- Risk buffer (patching, downtime, model regressions): 15–30% of (X+Y)
- Managed Redwood alternative: unit token price + optional Dedicated reservation line -> present delta and time-to-value comparison.

Technical-comparison talking points vs vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM stacks:
- vLLM (open framework, strong batching heuristics): Great for fast prototyping and single-model workloads. Weakness: multi-tenant production at scale needs careful KV cache management and complex autoscaling. Buy-line: "Great for PoC, less so for full production with mixed model types and enterprise rollouts."
- TGI (text-generation-inference wrappers): Good for MLFLOW-style model ops; still requires ops work to get latency/prefix caching stable across models. Buy-line: "TGI simplifies model packaging but doesn't eliminate operational drift—runtime tuning still required."
- TensorRT-LLM (highly-optimized kernels): Best latency/cost for supported architectures on NVIDIA hardware. Weakness: brittle across model changes, limited tooling for multi-model routing and evals. Buy-line: "Top raw perf but high maintenance and limited portability—great if you commit to a single model family and hardware stack."

Key operational risks to call out explicitly:
- Drift in model compatibility after upstream model changes (quantization regressions, operator changes).
- Tail-latency spikes from batch packing and garbage collection of KV caches.
- Silent quality regressions after quantization or kernel swaps—customers often lack systematic eval/rollout tooling.
- Cross-team burden: product teams expect "it just works" but platform teams bear toil.

Common buyer claims and suggested rebuttals (short scripts):
- Claim: "We can save 40% by running on spot instances + vLLM."
  Rebuttal: "Spot and vLLM help costs but the full picture needs SRE/Oncall, real-time evictions, and engineered fallbacks. Let's model expected spot eviction rate and the cost of the required reliability engineering—often larger than the nominal infra savings."
- Claim: "We want full data control so we must self-host."
  Rebuttal: "Understood—many enterprise customers choose Redwood Private to keep control over the network and keys while offloading runtime plumbing and lifecycle management. Can we map the exact controls you need and test a Private pilot?"
- Claim: "We have an infra team; this is not hard to own."
  Rebuttal: "Great. Ask them how many platform incidents they would accept monthly and who will build features like streaming, function routing, and automatic fallback. Also ask about the plan when you upgrade model families and quantization formats—these are recurring engineering tasks."

Sales hooks and win themes (short punchy lines):
- "Predictable inference economics, not surprise toil."
- "Ship features: function-calling and streaming without months of runtime changes."
- "SLA-backed latency tiers and seamless fallbacks across model variants and regions."
- "Hybrid path: start hosted, graduate to Dedicated, or run Private with our upgrades and SRE support."

Operational offer ideas to test with prospects (experiments for AE):
- 6-week pilot: measure 2 metrics—median tokens/sec and 99th tail latency on their real traffic. Redwood provides Dedicated burst credits & SRE onboarding.
- Brownfield migration guarantee: Redwood keeps old endpoints until parity tests pass (traffic shadowing + evals).
- Cost-compare workshop: we model 12 months TCO (infra + ops + risk) vs Redwood pricing, include migration friction and time-to-market penalty.

Open questions / hypotheses to validate with customers and field: (use as discovery prompts)
- At what token/month level do infra amortization benefits eclipse ops FTEs for 90% of prospects? (hypothesis: ~12–15B tokens/month with stable traffic patterns)
- How many customers are willing to trade a small latency increase (5–8%) for removing SRE burden? (hypothesis: most early product teams)
- Which regulated industries insist on air-gap vs those satisfied with Private + KMS? (hypothesis: finance + defense = air-gap; health + legal often satisfied with Private + audit logs)

Appendix / quick checklist for SEs in discovery calls:
- Ask for 30-day traffic profile, peak QPS, and token distribution by request length.
- Ask about model change cadence (how often models are swapped/retrained).
- Ask about SLOs (p50, p95, p99) and acceptable outage windows.
- Ask about internal platform FTEs available and willingness to hire for runtime tasks.
- Ask about compliance requirements (data residency, audit, encryption).

Notes & next steps:
- Convert this brief to a short two-slide battlecard for SDR/AEs with the 3 decision thresholds and a cost-model template.
- Run 5 customer interviews to validate token/month threshold hypothesis and the willingness-to-pay for managed fallbacks.
- SEs: capture three anonymized case studies (one small, one mid, one large) where self-hosting failed due to ops drift and one where it succeeded because of exclusive hardware commitment.

Raw/working items for follow-up (scratchpad):
- Pull anonymized infra invoices for 3 customers who moved from self-hosted -> managed.
- Get quantization failure logs from applied-ml infra to build a short "quantization risk" slide.
